{{< lifecycle-banner >}}

> **The short version.** OrgPath's value — a governed, deterministic
> organizational model that drives access, segmentation, and audit — does
> **not** depend on Microsoft Entra ID. The organizational *meaning* is
> vendor-neutral canon; only the *storage location* is vendor-specific, and
> that is handled by a small, swappable **binding profile** per platform. You
> adopt a new cloud or identity provider by writing a profile, not by forking
> the product. Provenance: [UIAO_193](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/UIAO_193_OrgPath_MultiCloud_Binding.md),
> [ADR-098](../../adr/adr-098-orgpath-vendor-neutral-binding-profiles.qmd),
> [ADR-099](../../adr/adr-099-orgpath-idp-binding-profile-expansion.qmd).

## The question this page answers

> *"We're not all-Microsoft. We have Okta (or Ping, or Keycloak, or Auth0)
> for identity, and workloads in AWS, GCP, and VMware. Is OrgPath only useful
> if we live in Entra ID?"*

No. OrgPath was designed from the start to separate **what your org structure
means** from **where that structure is stored**. The first is universal; the
second is the only part that changes per vendor — and it's deliberately the
small part.

## What travels, and what adapts

| Component | Portability | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **OrgPath codebook** (the canonical org hierarchy, in YAML + JSON Schema) | **Very high** | A pure data model. No vendor dependency. It is the single source of truth every platform is governed against. |
| **The OrgPath facets** (a governed set of org attributes: region, department, division, role, classification, lifecycle dates, clearance, account type, …) | **Very high** | Structured attribute values. Any directory, cloud, or workload platform that supports custom attributes, tags, or labels can hold them. |
| **Governance layer** (drift detection, evidence/OSCAL generation, codebook validation) | **Very high** | Sits *above* the identity provider. It reasons over facets, not over a vendor API. |
| **Event-driven recalculation** ("movers") | **High** | Triggered by attribute-change events (webhooks / SCIM events / polling) — mechanism, not vendor. |
| **Policy & segmentation targeting** | **Medium-high** | Facets map to each platform's own rules engine (dynamic groups, group rules, policy expressions, security tags). |
| **Storage location & per-vendor write APIs** | **Vendor-specific** | This is the *binding profile* — the deliberately small, swappable part. |

The first four rows are the bulk of the value and they are vendor-neutral.
Only the last row is platform-specific, and it is contained in a single
declarative file per target.

## How portability works: the binding-profile model

Two things are kept strictly separate:

1. **The facet is the *subject*.** What "Department = Finance" or
   "Classification = Contractor" *means* is defined once, in the codebook
   ([UIAO_151](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/UIAO_151_OrgPath_Codebook.md)).
   Every platform is governed against this same definition.
2. **The binding profile is the *storage map*.** For one target platform, a
   profile declares *where* each facet lives (an attribute name, a tag key, a
   label, a custom-attribute id) and how it is read and written. The facet
   model never changes; only the locator and the transport do.

Because the facet vocabulary is constant, a policy authored against facets —
*"Finance contractors below Secret clearance get step-up auth and session
limits"* — is meaningful no matter which platform stamped the subject. The
profile is the unit of projection; the facet predicate is the unit of policy.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The one-line portability claim
A new platform is onboarded by **writing a binding profile (a locator map) +
a transport** — mirroring the established AD-mapping / Graph / ARM pattern.
**No core change is required**, and there are **no separate products to buy or
fork**: profiles are additive within the single governed codebase.
:::

## Coverage today

The following targets are first-class binding-profile targets at the
Commercial / Moderate boundary. Each is specified in
[UIAO_193](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/UIAO_193_OrgPath_MultiCloud_Binding.md);
the storage contracts ship as executable canon, with per-vendor write
transports following on the established pattern.

| Target | Plane(s) | Where facets live | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Microsoft Entra ID** | identity, device | Directory extension attributes; Arc machine tags | Reference profile |
| **AWS** | identity, workload | IAM Identity Center attributes; resource tags | Specified |
| **GCP** | identity, workload | Cloud Identity attributes; resource labels | Specified |
| **VMware** | identity, workload, enforcement | Workspace ONE Access attributes; vSphere tags; NSX security groups | Specified |
| **Okta** | identity | Universal Directory custom attributes | Specified |
| **Generic LDAP** | identity | Directory attributes (schema-extension or reserved) | Specified |
| **Ping (PingOne)** | identity | PingOne directory custom attributes | Specified (ADR-099) |
| **Keycloak / Red Hat build** | identity | Keycloak user attributes | Specified (ADR-099) |
| **Auth0** | identity | User profile `app_metadata` | Specified (ADR-099) |

VMware is intentionally the three-plane proof: the *same* facet set projects
onto a user (Workspace ONE Access), a workload (a vSphere VM), and an
enforcement construct (an NSX group) — evidence that the contract is not
identity-provider-centric.

The first-class list is curated, not open-ended: each new target is a governed
decision (an ADR), which is why Ping/Keycloak/Auth0 arrived via
[ADR-099](../../adr/adr-099-orgpath-idp-binding-profile-expansion.qmd) rather
than as a quiet config change.

## Getting facets to where they're consumed: carriage

Storing a facet is one thing; getting it to the app or edge that enforces on
it is another — especially across mixed identity providers. Two open
mechanisms carry facets without locking you to one vendor:

- **SCIM 2.0 provisioning.** Where a target supports SCIM, facets ride as
  custom schema-extension attributes on the SCIM `User` resource — the
  standards-based provisioning path for the identity profiles.
- **Token claims (SAML / OIDC).** Facets project as custom claims in the
  tokens your apps and your secure-access (SASE/SSE) layer already consume, so
  every relying party sees the same organizational context regardless of which
  IdP minted the token. This is the federation analog of the certificate-based
  carriage used for network admission
  ([UIAO_012](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/UIAO_012_OrgPath_in_NAC_and_8021X.md))
  and the signal the access-decision layer
  ([UIAO_013](https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/blob/main/src/uiao/canon/UIAO_013_OrgPath_in_Zero_Trust_and_SASE.md))
  acts on.

## What stays the same no matter the platform

This is the part that makes portability *governable* rather than merely
*possible*:

- **One source of truth.** The codebook defines org structure once; every
  platform is reconciled against it.
- **Drift is portable.** The drift engine validates facet *values* against the
  codebook regardless of where they're stored — so a stale or out-of-policy
  facet surfaces as the same `DRIFT-IDENTITY` finding on Okta, Keycloak, or
  Entra. In a heterogeneous estate, that's the difference between org context
  you can attest to and org context you merely hope is correct.
- **Evidence is portable.** The same audit artifacts (codebook validation,
  drift classification, OSCAL output) hold across a mixed estate — you don't
  re-prove org-context accuracy per vendor.
- **Zero Trust subject is portable.** Facets are the vendor-independent policy
  subject: author a microsegmentation or access rule once against facets, and
  it projects onto each platform's native enforcement construct.

## What this means for a buyer

- You are **not** betting your governance model on a single identity vendor.
- You can run **multiple IdPs and multiple clouds** under one org model and one
  audit story.
- Adopting a new platform is **additive** — a profile, not a migration of the
  governance layer.
- The governance, drift, and evidence value you get on Microsoft is the **same
  value** you get on Okta, Ping, Keycloak, Auth0, AWS, GCP, or VMware.
